data.title: New Zealand's FMA tightens CFD leverage and suitability rules for retail traders
data.description:
New Zealand's Financial Markets Authority (FMA) has tightened the licence conditions for firms that issue derivatives to retail investors, introducing leverage limits and stricter suitability checks for products such as contracts for difference (CFDs) and margin forex.

The regulator announced the changes on 17 November. They take effect on 18 November 2027, giving licensed derivatives issuers a year to adjust their onboarding and margin systems.

"Derivatives can be useful financial products, but they can also expose investors to significant risks, particularly where leverage is involved," said FMA general counsel Liam Mason.

Suitability checks with teeth

The first change is to the existing suitability condition. From November 2027, issuers must gather enough information to assess whether a product is suitable for a retail investor before allowing them to trade it, and must not permit trading where a product is unsuitable or not understood, the FMA said.

According to a legal update from law firm MinterEllison, the test moves from whether an investor "has the ability to understand" a derivative to whether the issuer has taken all reasonable steps to "determine whether the retail investor understands" its risks.

The revised condition also removes the current discretion to go ahead with a trade after issuing a written warning to a client who has not supplied enough information, MinterEllison said. Firms will also have to keep records of their suitability assessments.

MinterEllison noted that an FMA sector risk assessment in December 2020 found a quarter of the derivatives issuers licensed at the time were not taking reasonable steps to make suitability assessments.

Leverage limits, with an opt-out

The second change is a new leverage condition. New Zealand has not previously imposed leverage limits on derivatives issuers.

Under the condition published by the FMA, over-the-counter derivatives offered to retail investors must require a minimum initial margin of:

  • 3.33% for major currency pairs;
  • 5% for minor currency pairs, major stock market indices and gold;
  • 10% for minor indices and commodities other than gold;
  • 20% for other underlyings;
  • 50% for cryptoassets.

That equates to maximum leverage of 30:1 on major currency pairs, falling to 2:1 on crypto. Issuers subject to the condition would also have to close out positions when a client's account equity falls below the required maintenance margin.

The condition is not a blanket cap, however. Firms can keep offering higher leverage if they have three protections in place: negative balance protection, which limits a firm's recourse to the money and property in the client's account; a mandatory close-out when a client's margin falls below 50% of the required level; and a board-approved framework for identifying and supporting vulnerable investors.

The FMA said the additional measures are designed to reduce the risk of significant losses "while preserving access to higher-risk products where appropriate safeguards are in place".

How it compares

The margin tiers mirror the retail CFD leverage limits that the European Securities and Markets Authority introduced across the EU in 2018 and that the UK's Financial Conduct Authority also applies. In those markets, however, the caps sit alongside the 50% close-out rule and negative balance protection rather than being an alternative to them.

New Zealand's approach therefore leaves room for issuers that already run Europe-style protections to continue offering higher leverage locally, provided they add a vulnerable investor framework. Traders comparing providers can see how leverage, protections and costs differ in our guides to the best CFD brokers and best forex brokers.

The FMA said the final conditions follow consultation in 2024 and 2025 and evidence from its supervisory work, complaints, disputes and court findings, and that it refined parts of its original proposals after industry feedback.

What happens next

Licensed derivatives issuers in New Zealand now have until 18 November 2027 to update client onboarding, record-keeping and margin close-out processes, or to put the three alternative protections in place.

data.title: SpaceX stock: why are lenders trying to stop Elon Musk's AI space plans?
data.description:
SpaceX faces fresh questions over its artificial intelligence expansion after lenders backing a reported $43 billion financing package sought assurances that Elon Musk would not launch the Nvidia chips securing the debt into orbit.

The proposed restrictions, reported by the Financial Times on Friday, reflect concerns that valuable computing equipment would be difficult to recover if SpaceX defaulted. Whether the provisions entered the final agreements remains unclear.

SpaceX stock (NASDAQ: SPCX) closed 3.53% lower at $138.43 on Thursday, before the lender concerns were widely reported.

The dispute highlights a growing tension between Musk's plans for orbital data centres and the practical demands of financing AI infrastructure.

SpaceX stock: Why lenders want Nvidia chips to stay on Earth

The financing, known as Project Saturn, supports the purchase of Nvidia processors for SpaceX's expanding AI business.

Investors bought more than $30 billion of debt on Thursday, with Bloomberg reporting a roughly $32 billion bond sale.

The largest portion is a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by approximately five years of lease payments for the GPUs.

The new securities reportedly yield about 8.3%, compared with roughly 7.2% on SpaceX debt maturing in 2031.

The structure offers lenders security in the underlying chips and contractual payments. But servers launched into orbit would be far harder to repossess, transport or sell after a default than equipment installed in a terrestrial data centre.

Rapid advances in semiconductor technology also mean their collateral value could diminish before the debt matures, heightening the importance of physical access.

"The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured," Shorecliff Asset Management chief investment officer Grant Nachman told the Financial Times, identifying potential demand from insurers seeking higher-yielding investment-grade debt.

Elon Musk's orbital data centres face an engineering test

Musk wants to place powerful computing systems aboard satellites, potentially using solar energy in orbit to support AI workloads without some of the land and electricity constraints facing Earth-based facilities.

Doing so would introduce problems conventional data centres rarely confront. Heat must be radiated into space, components must survive radiation and extreme conditions, and faulty equipment cannot readily be replaced.

Communications capacity and the cost of launch add further uncertainty.

Reusable Starship rockets could eventually make carrying substantial hardware into orbit more affordable.

SpaceX made progress in its November test programme, although the heavy-lift system has not established routine, economical reuse.

“Starship remains the enabling infrastructure” behind major opportunities, including orbital data centres and expanded Starlink deployments, KeyBanc analyst Mike Leshock told MarketWatch.

For now, SpaceX says its Apollo-backed GPU arrangement is intended for terrestrial computing.

That difference matters: financing assets in orbit may require protections fundamentally different from those supporting ordinary equipment leases.

What the financing dispute means for SpaceX stock

In October, SpaceX announced a binding commitment for an approximately $40 billion equipment lease with an Apollo-managed entity.

Deliveries of Nvidia Vera Rubin systems are expected to begin during the first half of 2027, subject to closing conditions.

The earlier lease and the reported $43 billion financing describe related arrangements, not two separate sums to be added together.

Investors remain divided on how much value to assign SpaceX's emerging AI business.

Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas reiterated an Overweight rating and $300 price target, with $170 of that target attributed to enterprise AI, according to TheStreet.

"On FY28, SPCX trades cheaper than the S&P500. Interesting," Jonas wrote in an earlier valuation note.

By contrast, Morningstar estimates fair value at $70, reflecting concerns about infrastructure spending and whether AI demand can justify the investment.

data.title: Here's why gold prices are crashing 9% in their worst week in eight months
data.description:
Gold prices sank to their lowest level since September 2025 on Friday, putting bullion on course for its steepest weekly decline in eight months as investors adjusted to the prospect of further US interest-rate increases.

Spot gold fell 2.7% to $3,525.25 an ounce by 05:04 GMT, extending its weekly slide to about 9.2%. December US gold futures dropped 4.3% to $3,526.

The retreat came even as Asian technology shares faced renewed selling pressure, a reminder that gold does not always benefit from market turmoil.

Gold price today: Fed outlook strengthens the dollar's grip

The dollar remained near a 19-month high, making bullion more expensive for buyers using other currencies. Rising US Treasury yields also offered investors an income-bearing alternative to gold.

Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October meeting, published on Wednesday, showed almost all policymakers anticipated further tightening to bring inflation towards the central bank's 2% target.

Markets assigned a 96.8% probability to a quarter-percentage-point rate increase in December, against a 3.2% chance of a half-point move, according to a Friday morning CME FedWatch snapshot.

Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson reinforced the case for higher rates on Thursday, describing October's pause as a matter of pace rather than a change in direction.

Fawad Razaqzada, a market analyst at FOREX.com, said in research published Thursday that rising real yields were particularly damaging for gold because it pays no interest. A meaningful recovery, he argued, may require a pause in the dollar's rally.

Gold price crash: Liquidations magnify the sell-off

The decline has accelerated as some investors close positions rather than wait for bullion to recover.

Capital.com analyst Kyle Rodda attributed part of the move to forced selling across financial markets, with persistent inflation and a stronger dollar adding to the pressure.

Mauricio Di Bartolomeo, co-founder of lending company Ledn, offered a related interpretation in comments published by The Wall Street Journal.

After gold's earlier gains, some holders may be choosing to realise profits and move into US Treasuries, which now offer comparatively attractive yields.

Other precious metals also declined. Spot silver dropped 3.5% to $41.25 an ounce, platinum lost 3.6% to $1,299.25 and palladium slid 3.3% to $879.47.

Separately, Swiss customs figures showed gold exports fell 34% in October to 109.7 tonnes, driven by fewer shipments to Britain.

The data illustrate changing physical bullion flows, rather than explaining Friday's price plunge on their own.

Is $3,500 the next test for gold price?

The speed of the retreat has brought $3,500 into focus.

Razaqzada warned in an assessment covered by Kitco that gold could test that level if expectations of tighter policy keep lifting yields and supporting the dollar.

That is a conditional technical risk, not a firm price prediction.

Gold has already fallen far enough to raise the prospect of a brief oversold rebound, but Razaqzada cautioned that weak momentum still favours sellers.

Traders will now look towards the Fed's 8–9 December meeting and the November US consumer inflation report scheduled for 10 December.

A softer inflation reading or a retreat in the dollar could help stabilise gold. Until then, bullion remains exposed to further selling driven by yields, currency movements and leveraged positions.

data.title: Why did Anthropic stock lose half its opening gains on IPO day?
data.description:
Anthropic stock (NASDAQ: ANT) lost roughly half their opening premium on Thursday as the artificial intelligence developer's record-breaking Nasdaq debut ran into valuation concerns and a sharp sell-off across Wall Street.

The Claude maker opened at $111.50, or 34.3% above its $83 initial public offering price, and reached $114.99. By the close, shares had retreated to $97.17, still 17.1% above the offer price.

That left investors who bought at the opening trade facing a 12.9% decline, despite a profitable first session for those allocated shares at the IPO price.

The reversal exposed the gap between demand for an AI listing and doubts about the price investors should pay.

Anthropic stock: A record debut loses its early momentum

Anthropic raised $81.34 billion by selling 980 million shares, after increasing the offering and pricing it above the original $70 to $78 range.

The total includes shares sold by investors, meaning not all proceeds will go to the company. Anthropic has also arranged a separate $26 billion private placement involving major technology groups.

Trading began shortly before noon in New York. The opening surge briefly lifted Anthropic's fully diluted valuation above $2 trillion, against about $1.5 trillion at the offering price.

But the rush did not last. Shares lost $14.33 between the open and the close, surrendering just over half of the initial $28.50 premium above the IPO price.

"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising," University of Florida professor Jay Ritter told CBS News, citing differing views of Anthropic's future profitability.

The pullback is consistent with investors reassessing what to pay after an unusually strong opening, although individual sellers' motives cannot be established from trading data alone.

Anthropic IPO news: A $2 trillion valuation meets costly ambitions

Anthropic's business is expanding at a remarkable pace. Revenue reached $33.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up more than twelvefold from a year earlier.

Even so, the company recorded an operating loss of about $1.3 billion. It also disclosed $900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, mainly tied to computing infrastructure, extending over multiple years.

Some $451.6 billion of those commitments is expected before the end of 2030. The figure is not an immediate cash bill, but underscores the investment required to keep developing and serving sophisticated AI models.

At Thursday's opening price, the company's valuation approached $2 trillion. By the close, it had fallen to approximately $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

"We got in at a far lower valuation through the private markets," Strategy Asset Managers chief executive Tom Hulick told Investing.com, explaining why his firm was not adding at the debut price.

His stance illustrates the difference between believing in Anthropic's growth and finding its shares attractive at any price.

The wider AI sell-off makes investors cautious

Anthropic's debut did not reverse weakness elsewhere in technology stocks. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.25% on Thursday, while the S&P 500 lost 2.02%.

Nvidia declined 3.3% and Advanced Micro Devices shed 7.7%, amid worries about AI spending, financing costs and richly valued technology businesses.

"Don't mistake one blockbuster deal for an all-clear signal," technology analyst Luke Lango warned in The Wall Street Journal.

Some investors are reassessing the cost of financing AI infrastructure as US interest-rate expectations rise. Higher borrowing costs can pressure richly valued growth shares, especially when profits depend on spending years ahead.

Competition from OpenAI, Google and lower-cost models adds another reason for investors to demand evidence of returns.

data.title: Why are Samsung and SK Hynix crashing after Nvidia and AMD's sharp losses?
data.description:
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix stock plunged nearly 6% on Friday as Wall Street's technology sell-off spread to Seoul, deepening investor concerns about the profitability of the artificial intelligence boom.

Samsung fell 6.09% and SK Hynix dropped 5.75% by 11:20 am local time. South Korea's benchmark KOSPI tumbled 4.24% to 4,919.86, surrendering Thursday's recovery.

The declines followed a bruising US session in which Nvidia lost 3.3% and Advanced Micro Devices shed 7.7%.

The scale of the Korean sell-off reflects more than weakness in American chip stocks.

Foreign investors are pulling money out despite strong memory-chip earnings, raising questions about how much investors will pay for future AI growth.

Nvidia, AMD stocks' losses shake confidence in AI

Nvidia's slide came just days after it reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and forecast approximately $130 billion for the following quarter.

The strong numbers confirmed that demand for advanced AI processors remains robust, but failed to settle concerns about expensive data-centre projects and their eventual returns.

AMD faced additional selling after short-seller-linked Hunterbrook Media raised questions about its relationships with Chinese technology companies and potential exposure to US export restrictions.

AMD denied the allegations, which have not been established as violations.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.25% on Thursday, while Anthropic's highly anticipated stock-market debut offered little relief.

The AI developer closed 17.1% above its IPO price, but enthusiasm for that listing did not extend across the sector.

Samsung and SK Hynix supply memory used in AI servers, making their shares sensitive to changes in investors' expectations for computing investment.

Aberdeen Investments portfolio manager Isaac Thong described a shift “away from anything linked to AI into anything defensive, high quality and stable,” according to Reuters.

Foreign withdrawals outweigh powerful chip earnings

The pressure is particularly acute in South Korea, where overseas investors have been selling shares for months.

By late Friday morning, foreigners had sold a net 760.54 billion won of KOSPI stocks, while institutions offloaded another 443.61 billion won. Retail investors bought roughly 1.01 trillion won, but could not prevent the decline.

According to Reuters, foreign investors were heading for a seventh consecutive month of net selling, with cumulative withdrawals of approximately $115.2 billion.

That exodus contrasts with record profits at Samsung and SK Hynix, supported by high-bandwidth memory demand and tight production capacity.

Both companies have also announced substantial shareholder-return programmes, although the winding down of some buybacks could weaken an important source of demand for their shares.

Samsung expects memory supplies to remain tight through 2028; SK Hynix has pointed to shortages lasting even longer.

Samsung Futures analyst Jung Hee-chan told MoneyToday that investors need convincing that exceptional chip profits can endure before stronger earnings forecasts translate into higher share prices.

Can battered Korean chip shares recover?

Friday's slide pushed the KOSPI back below 5,000 after Thursday's 1.39% rebound. For traders, reclaiming that threshold would provide an early sign that selling pressure is easing, rather than proof of a lasting recovery.

Thursday's rebound in Samsung and SK Hynix had been supported by local buying, even as overseas investors remained wary.

Friday's retreat suggests bargain hunters alone cannot stabilise the benchmark if international funds continue reducing exposure.

Goldman Sachs has reduced its 12-month KOSPI target to 7,500, though the bank still sees scope for Korean shares to recover from discounted valuations.

Kiwoom Securities analyst Han Ji-young told Seoul Economic Daily that portfolio rotation around Anthropic's IPO could prove short-lived and that bargain hunting might help limit losses.

data.title: Evening digest: Anthropic makes historic debut, AMD falls 8%
data.description:
Anthropic shares surged 34.3% initially after making their Nasdaq debut, pushing the AI company's market valuation above $2 trillion.

AMD fell 8% after an investigation by Hunterbrook Media alleged that its firmware was being used by a blacklisted Chinese server maker and related businesses.

Gold dropped to a 14-month low as a stronger dollar and expectations of higher US interest rates weighed on bullion.

Oil prices recovered as reports of tanker disruptions and escalating tensions around the Strait of Hormuz raised concerns about Middle Eastern supply.

Anthropic stock jumps 34% in record IPO debut

Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT, opening at $111.50 a share after pricing its IPO at $83.

The company raised more than $81 billion through the sale of approximately 980 million shares, making it the largest IPO on record.

Shares climbed 34.3% after opening, taking the company's valuation above $2 trillion. This placed Anthropic behind Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet and Amazon in market capitalisation.

The stock pared gains and was trading 14% up at the time of writing.

The offering was led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, with JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Barclays also serving as underwriters.

The debut is significant for the wider AI sector because Anthropic is the first major AI laboratory to go public.

Its shares could become a benchmark for investor appetite towards AI companies as markets assess whether substantial spending on models and computing infrastructure can generate sustainable returns.

Co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei rang the Nasdaq opening bell.

Dario Amodei reiterated the company's commitment to AI safety, saying it would not bend to business or political pressure.

Anthropic could also benefit from Nasdaq's revised index inclusion rules, which allow eligible large-cap companies to qualify for fast-track inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 after 15 trading days.

Intropic estimates that index-tracking funds could purchase around 333 million shares across four dates during the first month.

AMD stock falls 8% on China exposure allegations

AMD shares declined 8% after Hunterbrook Media alleged that the company's firmware was being used by IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker placed on the US government's Entity List in March 2025.

The investigation identified at least six newer versions of AMD firmware in IEIT products after the blacklisting.

It also alleged that three companies in China, Singapore and California offered servers containing closely matching firmware.

Hunterbrook said corporate filings indicated links between IEIT and some of these businesses.

The report also raised questions about AMD licensing income from two Chinese chip ventures previously blacklisted by US authorities.

The allegations have drawn attention to AMD's exposure to export restrictions at a time when investors have viewed it as an alternative to Nvidia.

Hunterbrook disclosed that its affiliated investment firm was short AMD shares and held long positions in comparable securities.

Gold hits 14-month low as rate expectations rise

Spot gold fell 1.45% to $3,668.27 an ounce, after touching $3,667.19, its lowest level since September 2025. US gold futures settled 1.85% lower at $3,672.50.

A stronger US dollar and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy weighed on bullion.

The dollar index reached its highest level since April 2025, making dollar-priced gold more expensive for overseas buyers.

Markets were pricing in a 94% chance of a 25-basis-point rate increase in December and a 6% probability of a 50-basis-point move.

Higher interest rates reduce the appeal of non-yielding assets such as gold.

Silver, platinum and palladium also declined.

Oil rises as Strait of Hormuz risks return

Brent crude gained 0.29% to $92.22 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate rose 0.58% to $83.74.

Reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz supported prices after the previous session's decline, which was driven by rising US inventories and expectations of a supply surplus.

Iran's navy said two oil tankers hit naval mines and exploded in the strait.

Meanwhile, Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh added to regional tensions.

However, concerns about ample supply continued to limit gains.

Saudi crude exports rose nearly 21% in September to 5.38 million barrels per day, while a larger-than-expected increase in US inventories reinforced concerns about a potential surplus.

data.title: Aswath Damodaran values Anthropic at $76 a share, below its $83 IPO price
data.description:
Aswath Damodaran, the New York University finance professor widely known as the 'Dean of Valuation', estimates Anthropic's intrinsic value at approximately $76 per share, below the artificial intelligence company's $83 initial public offering (IPO) price.

In an updated valuation published ahead of the company's Nasdaq debut, Damodaran estimated Anthropic's aggregate equity value at approximately $1.35 trillion.

His calculations incorporated the company's latest financial results, higher computing costs and the possibility of tighter AI regulations.

Anthropic raised $81 billion in its IPO, making it the largest offering of all time.

The company priced its shares at $83 apiece, above its initial guidance range of $70 to $78.

The stock opened on Nasdaq at $111.50 under the ticker ANT giving it a $2 trillion valuation, before giving up some gains to trade at $96.33 at the time of writing.

Damodaran's assessment suggests that the stock's offering price was already above his estimated intrinsic value, while its subsequent market price represented a further premium.

Damodaran lowers Anthropic valuation over rising costs and regulatory risks

Damodaran had initially valued Anthropic's equity at approximately $1.475 trillion in a November 2 analysis.

However, developments over the following 15 days prompted him to revise his assumptions.

The updated prospectus provided third-quarter financial information, while the US midterm election results raised questions about the future economics of the AI industry.

In particular, Damodaran expects data centres to become more expensive to build and AI regulations to become more stringent.

He reduced his assumption for sales generated per dollar of capital invested during the first five years from $3 to $2.75, reflecting higher expected infrastructure spending.

He also increased the anticipated regulatory drag on operating margins, adjusting his assumptions from 5% to 6%, with the target operating margin set at 26.5%.

Damodaran explained that these changes would increase the company's reinvestment requirements and reduce its expected cash flows.

"I do not want to overreact to the election results, but I do think it is prudent to assume that building data centers will become more expensive," he wrote.

Share count complicates Anthropic's intrinsic value calculation

A significant part of Damodaran's analysis focused on the difficulty of determining Anthropic's actual share count.

He argued that the presence of multiple share classes, restricted stock, and employee stock options makes it difficult to arrive at an accurate per-share valuation.

According to his analysis, Anthropic's share count could range from approximately 14.88 billion shares under the primary share method to 17.68 billion under the fully diluted approach.

The company has 1.026 billion restricted shares subject to a four-year vesting period and 1.774 billion outstanding options, of which 1.082 billion are already vested.

Damodaran argued that simply using either the primary or fully diluted share count could produce misleading results.

Instead, he favours an option-adjusted approach, which estimates the value of outstanding options and deducts that amount from aggregate equity value before dividing it by the primary and restricted shares.

"I would suggest viewing the option-adjusted value per share as the number closest to the truth," he wrote.

His calculations produced a range of values, with the primary share approach generating a higher estimate and the fully diluted method producing a lower one.

The option-adjusted valuation stood at approximately $76 per share, compared with the $83 IPO price.

Anthropic's growth prospects underpin long-term valuation

Despite the downward revision, Damodaran's valuation model assumes substantial growth for Anthropic over the coming years.

His assumptions project revenue growth of 190% in the next year, followed by 42% annual growth during years two to five.

Revenue growth subsequently moderates as the company matures.

The model also assumes that operating margins will improve as the company gains pricing power from premium AI products and computing costs grow more slowly than revenues.

Damodaran expects Anthropic's operating margin to reach 26.5% over time, while its cost of capital gradually declines as the company becomes more established.

His analysis also considers the substantial computing commitments the company has made, including lease, purchase, and infrastructure obligations.

He incorporated a 10% probability of failure into the valuation to account for the risks associated with those commitments.

Beyond the financial assumptions, Damodaran raised concerns about Anthropic's unusual voting structure.

He noted that a founder-owned share carries 50.01% of voting rights in perpetuity.

He compared the arrangement with government-held golden shares in privatised companies, arguing that concentrating such significant voting power in a single share could create risks.

Overall, Damodaran's analysis highlights the distinction between Anthropic's long-term growth potential and the price investors are willing to pay for its shares.

While his model anticipates substantial revenue expansion and improving profitability, higher infrastructure costs, regulatory uncertainty, and share dilution remain important considerations in assessing its valuation.

data.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei defends $900B AI spending and safety strategy after IPO
data.description:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei outlined the company's long-term growth strategy, artificial intelligence (AI) safety priorities and path to profitability following its stock market debut on Thursday.

Speaking to CNBC after the company's initial public offering (IPO), the siblings discussed how Anthropic intends to balance its rapid expansion with responsible AI development, rising computing costs and the expectations of public-market investors.

Anthropic sees long-term value in balancing growth with AI safety

Dario Amodei said the company's understanding of scaling laws helped establish the potential of AI models, although the economic implications became clearer only as the technology developed.

He described the company's approach to pacing AI development as a way to balance technological progress with safety considerations.

"We could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely," Amodei said, explaining the company's approach to developing increasingly capable models.

He argued that this strategy could also benefit investors over the longer term, as companies that establish trust with customers and enterprises could be better positioned to succeed.

"The company that builds the safest, that has trust of the customers and the enterprises of the world, I think that is the company that's going to be both best for society and, in the long run, I hope, best for the performance of the company," he added.

Daniela Amodei also highlighted the company's public benefit corporation structure, which legally requires it to balance shareholder interests with its commitment to public benefit.

She said the structure reflects the founders' intention to build a company that generates economic value while ensuring its technology benefits society.

She added that Anthropic considers safety a central part of its mission and believes the technology carries both significant opportunities and real risks.

"Anthropic has been a safety company, a safety-first company from day one," Daniela Amodei said. "The promise is incredible, and the risks are real."

Frontier AI models and computing costs remain central to strategy

Discussing competition from OpenAI, open-weight models and technology companies developing their own AI systems, Dario Amodei said Anthropic believes the biggest economic opportunities remain concentrated at the AI frontier.

He argued that improvements in cognitive capabilities can unlock applications beyond chatbots, including coding, biology and robotics.

"The economic value of things further along the frontier is so much larger than things earlier in the frontier that that's where most of the value accumulates," he said.

He also said developing frontier models gives Anthropic an advantage in producing smaller and more efficient models that can compete on price.

As an example, he cited the company's Haiku 5.5 model, saying Anthropic had reduced its price by four times compared with Haiku 4.5.

Meanwhile, Daniela Amodei addressed concerns about the infrastructure required to support the company's expansion.

She said Anthropic wants local communities to have a voice in data centre development and stressed that additional electricity costs should not be passed on to consumers.

"We have already committed to matching whatever price differential might happen from an electricity grid perspective, we pay for," she said.

Dario Amodei addresses $900B commitments and profitability

Anthropic has $900 billion in infrastructure commitments, which is expected to put pressure on its path to profitability.

Dario Amodei said the spending commitments were spread across several years and don't look large when compared to the cash the company has and the revenue it's making.

"If you look at the amount of cash we have on the balance sheet and the amount of revenue that we're already making per year, suddenly, those commitments don't seem so large," he said.

Amodei said Anthropic generally tries to estimate its computing requirements conservatively and purchase additional capacity from the spot market when necessary.

However, he maintained that spending on research and development and training more capable models remained worthwhile because of the economic returns the company had historically generated.

"The returns to that are so high that we are willing to put in place these very large compute spends because, historically, we have seen over and over again that it pays off," he added.

The CEO also discussed the possibility of using debt financing in the future.

He said Anthropic hoped to achieve an investment-grade credit rating and viewed debt as a financing instrument it could eventually use.

On the subject of partnerships, Daniela Amodei highlighted the company's relationships with Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, saying access to multiple computing partners had been a strategic advantage.

Dario Amodei also said the company was satisfied with its work with SpaceX, which provides computing capacity.

Addressing investor expectations following the IPO, the CEO said Anthropic would remain focused on its underlying business rather than short-term share price movements.

"We always want to under promise and overdeliver," he said, describing a principle that guides the company's internal operations and its approach to investors.

He added that the long-term fundamentals of the business mattered more than daily, weekly or monthly market movements.

Anthropic raised $81 billion in its IPO, making it the largest offering of all time.

The company priced its shares at $83 apiece, above its initial guidance range of $70 to $78.

The stock opened on Nasdaq at $111.50, under the ticker ANT.

The stock gave up some gains and was trading at $98.32 at the time of writing.

The strong debut marked an important milestone for the AI company, which has attracted significant investor interest amid growing concerns about the sustainability of technology companies' AI spending.

data.title: Anthropic pops 34% to cross $2 trillion valuation in historic Nasdaq debut
data.description:
Anthropic ANT made its stock market debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $111.50 per share, raising more than $81 billion in what is the largest initial public offering on record.

Shares jumped 34.3% after opening, pushing the artificial intelligence company's market valuation above $2 trillion.

This placed Anthropic behind only Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet and Amazon in terms of market capitalization.

The IPO carries significant implications for the AI trade, as Anthropic becomes the first major AI lab to go public. Analysts expect Anthropic shares to become a proxy for the broader AI trade.

The listing comes at a time when concerns are mounting over the sustainability of the AI boom, with questions further intensifying amid the ongoing Nvidia leadership turmoil.

The Claude maker sold 980 million shares at an IPO price of $83 apiece, above the previously marketed range of $70 to $78.

The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

The IPO was led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, with JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Barclays also listed in the prospectus as underwriters.

Anthropic reiterates commitment to AI safety

Anthropic co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei rang the Nasdaq opening bell, marking the public listing of the company behind the Claude chatbot.

Dario Amodei used the occasion to reiterate the company's commitment to AI safety, saying: "We will not bend to either business or political pressure."

He also pledged that Anthropic would remain "obsessed with safety" as it seeks to avoid potentially catastrophic risks associated with artificial intelligence.

The debut comes as investors continue to assess how much value can be created by companies developing increasingly powerful AI models, even as concerns persist over the scale of spending required to train and operate them.

Nasdaq rules could provide another boost

Anthropic could receive a further boost from changes to Nasdaq's index inclusion rules introduced earlier this year.

The revised methodology allows large-cap companies to qualify for fast-track inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 after just 15 days of trading.

The change was implemented before SpaceX's June listing and could accelerate demand from passive funds tracking the benchmark.

Research group Intropic estimates that index-tracking funds will purchase around 333 million Anthropic shares across four dates during the first month of trading.

That represents approximately 30% of the 1.1 billion shares in the offering, including the greenshoe option.

Anthropic revenue surges as losses widen

Anthropic filed its prospectus last month, revealing a sharp acceleration in revenue, which surged around 1,200% during the first nine months of the year.

For the first half of 2026, the filing showed revenue of $16.29 billion, up from $1.16 billion a year earlier.

The company's reported net loss for the first half of 2026 was $80.748 billion, compared with a net loss of $41.965 billion for the full year 2025.

While the headline figures appear alarming, much of the reported loss was attributed to an accounting practice.

data.title: AMD stock falls 7% as Hunterbrook alleges links to blacklisted Chinese firm
data.description:
AMD stock fell 7% on Thursday after Hunterbrook Media, an investigative publication affiliated with short seller Hunterbrook Capital, alleged that the chipmaker's firmware was being used by a blacklisted Chinese company and three businesses linked to it.

The report claimed that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker, had incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products after being placed on the US government's export blacklist.

Hunterbrook also alleged that three other server companies with links to IEIT offered products containing closely matching firmware, raising questions about whether servers designed by the blacklisted company were being sold through other businesses.

The revelations were made in a report called 'AMD has its own China problem'.

Hunterbrook Media disclosed that, at the time of publication, its affiliated investment firm Hunterbrook Capital was short AMD shares and held long positions in a basket of comparable securities.

The report drew parallels with the controversy surrounding Nvidia's sales of advanced chips to Chinese companies and questioned whether AMD could genuinely be considered a safer alternative to its larger rival.

AMD's China exposure comes under scrutiny

The firm has questioned a growing perception that AMD is a less risky way to gain exposure to the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom amid scrutiny of Nvidia's China business.

The firm highlighted that AMD shares gained nearly 45% in the five sessions through November 12, the day Nvidia announced CEO Jensen Huang's resignation in what CNBC reported was a board decision to oust him.

William Blair and Oppenheimer also upgraded AMD during that period, according to Hunterbrook.

However, the publication argued that investors may be underestimating AMD's exposure to the same geopolitical and regulatory risks facing Nvidia.

As of the November 18 close, AMD traded at around 30 times its estimated earnings for the next fiscal year, compared with approximately nine times for Nvidia, based on analyst estimates published by Yahoo Finance.

"The Bear Cave believes investors are trading one cousin’s problems for the other’s," the report said, referring to Jensen Huang's relationship with AMD chief Lisa Su, who is his cousin.

The Bear Cave is an investigative newsletter owned by Hunterbrook Media.

IEIT allegedly used AMD firmware after blacklisting

Hunterbrook said the US Commerce Department placed IEIT on its Entity List in March 2025.

The designation means that exports of items covered by US export controls to the company require a licence, with the department's stated policy being to deny such applications.

Despite the restrictions, IEIT has incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products since being blacklisted, according to the investigation.

The latest version identified by Hunterbrook appeared in an updated product listing posted on October 19.

The report also identified three companies that sell servers built around AMD chips under their own brands: Maginfra in China, Kaytus in Singapore and Aivres in California.

"Hunterbrook found that the firmware they offer is nearly identical to IEIT’s, suggesting they may be selling servers designed by the blacklisted company. Corporate filings point the same way: IEIT’s 2022 annual report listed Aivres, then called Inspur Systems, as a subsidiary. Kaytus’s own audited accounts name IEIT as its ultimate parent company," it said.

The investigation also highlighted other alleged links between AMD and entities subject to US restrictions.

Hunterbrook said AMD reported $67 million in licensing income in 2025 that the publication traced to two Chinese chip ventures blacklisted in 2019.

It also identified a server from Cancon, an alias of the blacklisted company Suma, in AMD's February 2026 product catalogue.

"In sum: AMD appears no less at risk from China chip restrictions than Nvidia, despite the recent surge of positive coverage," Hunterbrook said.

Potential changes to export rules could add pressure

The report also warned that changes to US export regulations could expose AMD to additional restrictions on its international business.

A suspension of a rule that would extend export restrictions to foreign companies at least 50% owned by blacklisted entities is due to expire on January 10, 2027.

If implemented, the provision could expand restrictions to Kaytus and other foreign companies in which IEIT holds at least a 50% stake, it said.

Separately, a newly released interim final rule, which takes effect on Thursday, will require licences for advanced chips shipped to Singapore and four other countries.

The potential impact on AMD could be significant given its business in the region.

The company recorded $4.28 billion in billings to customers in Singapore during fiscal 2025, accounting for more than 10% of its total sales.

"For AMD, this could mean additional licensing requirements that can delay or block sales," Hunterbrook said.
